Combined with progressive fatigue and pruritus, this strongly suggests cholestatic liver disease — such as primary biliary cholangitis (PBC), primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC), or drug-induced or malignancy-related biliary obstruction. This strongly supports intra- or extrahepatic biliary obstruction or chronic cholestatic liver disease (e.g., PBC, PSC). Next, we need to assess for autoimmune etiology — anti-mitochondrial antibodies (AMA) are >95% sensitive and highly specific for PBC. Also, imaging is needed to rule out structural biliary obstruction (e.g., stones, stricture, tumor). Ultrasound is first-line, non-invasive, and widely available for evaluating biliary ducts and liver parenchyma.

Since AMA is a critical serologic test for PBC — the most common cause of chronic cholestasis in middle-aged women — and ultrasound can detect ductal dilation or obstruction, both are essential.
